**Logitech MX Keypad:** Configurable for specific AI and productivity workflows, including GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Microsoft 365 apps.
**Insta360 Link 2 Pro:** A 4K webcam featuring AI-based automatic framing, group tracking, and integrated noise cancellation for video conferencing.
**Autonomous Desk Pro:** Uses integrated sensors to track sitting/standing ratios and room CO2 levels, providing activity insights via an AI interface.

title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
author: Jess Weatherbed
contentSnippet: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access. “We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.” Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system. [Image: Signal’s app security settings on Android devices will display this message for the screenshot-blocking feature. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/protecting-your-privacy-2.png?quality=90&strip=all] Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed

summary.tldr:
Signal is implementing a restrictive policy on Android and iOS to block screenshot capabilities, aiming to prevent OS-level AI agents like Google Gemini and Apple’s Siri from scraping user messages. Signal President Meredith Whittaker stated that current operating system architectures allow AI agents to access on-screen data, which fundamentally undermines the app's privacy guarantees. While users can manually re-enable screenshots in the app settings, Signal warns that this action exposes message content to AI analysis and voids the platform's privacy protections.

Signal characterizes the current OS-level integration of AI as an 'existential threat' to application-layer privacy, noting that developers lack granular tools to restrict AI access without degrading core user experiences. The company specifically cited the inability to implement these protections on macOS due to a lack of developer-facing controls. Signal is calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide standardized technical tools and transparent documentation regarding how AI agents interact with application data, specifically highlighting concerns over accessibility settings being used as a 'skeleton key' for data extraction. This move follows Signal's previous efforts to block Microsoft’s Recall feature from accessing encrypted chats.
takeaways: **Core Mechanism:** Signal is disabling screenshot functionality on Android and iOS to prevent AI assistants from reading on-screen content.

**Developer Limitations:** Signal reports that major OS providers (Google, Apple, Microsoft) fail to provide robust APIs for developers to restrict AI data access without compromising app functionality.
**Platform Disparity:** The screenshot-blocking protection is currently unavailable on macOS due to the lack of necessary developer controls provided by Apple.
**Security Warning:** Signal explicitly warns that re-enabling screenshot capabilities in app settings will expose user data to AI agents and break the app's privacy guarantees.

**Industry Advocacy:** Signal is demanding that OS vendors provide 'simple technical tools' and documentation to prevent third-party agents from using accessibility settings to bypass application-level security.

title: Combatting adversarial distillation
author: OpenAI News
contentSnippet:
November 20, 2026 Combatting adversarial distillation How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly important role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

W e’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming , we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Why distillation is a safety issue

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answ

summary.tldr:
OpenAI detailed its methods for combatting adversarial distillation, a process where malicious actors extract frontier model capabilities and internal reasoning traces to train unprotected student models. Focusing on dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, the company outlined risks where transferred skills enable offensive capabilities previously blocked by original model safeguards.

To counter protected reasoning extraction, OpenAI updated its defenses in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal adaptive evaluations using automated red-teaming, the attack success rate dropped from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards. The defense architecture spans request-level controls—including adversarial training, input/output classifiers covering tool-call arguments, and API-level restrictions tying encrypted reasoning to specific conversation histories—and campaign-level investigations tracking coordinated extraction patterns across user and organization boundaries.
takeaways: **Red-Teaming Benchmark Improvement:** The average attack success rate for recovering protected reasoning fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with updated safeguards during internal adaptive evaluations.
**Model Generations Evaluated:** The defense updates and evaluations specifically target the GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol model families.

**Exact Reasoning vs. Summaries:** Internal studies showed that student models fine-tuned on exact reasoning traces outperformed students trained on reasoning summaries after supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

**API and Tool-Call Safeguards:** Output classifiers scan both assistant messages and tool-call arguments to prevent reasoning leakage, while API controls tie encrypted reasoning strictly to its originating conversation history and prevent older model families from reading GPT-6.2 reasoning.

title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
author: Yimeng Liu, Eric Isbrandt, Felix Katzenburg, Kevin P. Greenman, Han Hao, Yang Cao, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yimeng Liu , Eric Isbrandt , Felix Katzenburg , Kevin P. Greenman , Han Hao , Yang Cao , Varinia Bernales , Alán Aspuru-Guzik

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

summary.tldr:
Researchers led by Alán Aspuru-Guzik at the University of Toronto have developed an authorization-bounded AI agent architecture designed to bridge the 'Analyze-to-Design' gap in self-driving laboratories (SDLs). The system integrates into the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, specifically managing measurement selection and data interpretation while enforcing strict human-in-the-loop authorization for state-changing physical hardware operations. By ensuring all actions are validated and auditable, the architecture aims to move SDLs toward safer, unsupervised operation.

The team validated the architecture using a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument to screen oxidants for organic dye synthesis. The agent successfully submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, and identified failed experiments. Its oxidant ranking matched traditional scripted peak integration, and human chemists verified the agent's spectral interpretations. In simulated replays of LC-MS data, the agent identified the highest-yielding condition in approximately seven injections, compared to a random-order average of 14.5, and consistently succeeded when granted a limit of eight or more injections.
takeaways: **Architecture Focus:** The system targets the Analyze-Design interface of the DMTA cycle to enable autonomous measurement selection and data interpretation.
**Safety Mechanism:** The framework implements an authorization-bounded design, requiring human validation for any state-changing operations on physical laboratory hardware.
**Performance Metric:** In simulated LC-MS campaigns, the agent identified the highest-yielding condition in ~7 injections, outperforming the 14.5-injection average of random selection.
**Validation:** The agent's oxidant ranking and failure detection were cross-validated against scripted peak integration and expert review by organic chemists.

title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
author: Nianjun Zhou, Dhaval Patel
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.25070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced the 'CodeReAct agent,' an LLM-based framework designed to automate industrial maintenance workflows through natural language interaction. By standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls, the framework enables autonomous knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and predictive work order generation. The system is designed to replace manual data science intervention by automating complex analytical tasks, specifically targeting the interpretation of maintenance logs and equipment telemetry.

The framework operates on a 'Thought-Action-Observation' loop, where the agent generates executable code during the Action phase to perform data analysis. In a case study focused on chiller maintenance, the agent processed multiple years of historical work orders, alerts, and anomaly data to identify patterns and trends. The system demonstrates the ability to translate human utterances into actionable insights, effectively bridging the gap between unstructured maintenance data and structured decision-making in industrial engineering environments.
takeaways: **Framework Architecture:** The CodeReAct agent utilizes a Thought-Action-Observation loop to automate analytical tasks and generate executable code.
**Data Standardization:** The system converts raw industrial data into standardized business objects (BOs) to facilitate API-driven analysis.
**Case Study Application:** The framework was validated using multi-year maintenance data from chiller systems to identify anomalies and predict work orders.
**Operational Goal:** The primary objective is to reduce reliance on manual data scientist involvement for routine industrial maintenance analysis.

title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
author: Dhriti Verma, Kanthi Sarpatwar, Vinicius Lima, Dzung Phan, Jayant Kalagnanam
contentSnippet:
Authors: Dhriti Verma , Kanthi Sarpatwar , Vinicius Lima , Dzung Phan , Jayant Kalagnanam

Abstract: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Dhriti Verma, Kanthi Sarpatwar, Vinicius Lima, Dzung Phan, and Jayant Kalagnanam have introduced SailSearch, a human-guided workflow utilizing two language-model agents to accelerate algorithmic research in combinatorial optimization. The framework focuses on two primary problem domains: the Market Split problem and the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem. By leveraging LLM-assisted guidance, the researchers developed a randomized algorithm for Market Split that dynamically partitions computation between enumeration and continued lattice basis reduction.

In performance testing on the QOBLIB benchmark, the SailSearch-driven algorithm achieved the first reported CPU-only solutions for 18 of 33 previously unsolved instances. Across 156 total benchmark instances, the system consistently solved between 130 and 133 instances per random seed within a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For the MIS domain, the authors utilized a generator to create graphs with planted XOR constraints and certified optima. Testing against standard solvers on seven instances ranging from 1,752 to 3,996 vertices revealed that existing solvers fell short of the certified optima by 5 to 15 vertices during eight-hour execution windows.
takeaways: **Market Split Performance:** Solved 130–133 of 156 QOBLIB instances per seed using a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores.
**QOBLIB Breakthroughs:** Achieved the first CPU-only solutions for 18 of 33 previously open instances.
**MIS Benchmark Gap:** Standard solvers failed to reach certified optima on seven MIS instances (1,752–3,996 vertices), missing by 5 to 15 vertices in eight-hour runs.
**Methodology:** Utilizes a dual-agent LLM workflow to guide randomized search strategies and lattice basis reduction.

title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
author: John Wu, Rushi Qiang, Yuchen Zhuang, Guowang Li, Girish Narayanswamy, Max Xu, Sam Schmidgall, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, Jimeng Sun, Daniel McDuff, Bo Dai, Xin Liu
contentSnippet:
Authors: John Wu , Rushi Qiang , Yuchen Zhuang , Guowang Li , Girish Narayanswamy , Max Xu , Sam Schmidgall , Mark Malhotra , Shwetak Patel , Jimeng Sun , Daniel McDuff , Bo Dai , Xin Liu

Abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

summary.tldr:
Researchers from a multi-institutional team including Google, University of Washington, and Georgia Tech have introduced BuggyMLE, a framework designed to evaluate and train AI agents on complex, repository-level machine learning engineering (MLE) tasks. The authors developed the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a metric utilizing ten structural features—such as repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size—to predict agent solve rates with an R² of 0.951. By leveraging CCI, the team synthesized over 6,600 bug-injected repository variants across 222 source repositories, totaling nearly 260,000 lines of injected code to simulate realistic debugging and development environments.

Using this data, the researchers created BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, a difficulty-graded benchmark that reveals a sharp performance decline in current AI models, with top solve rates dropping from 95% to 9% as task difficulty increases. To address these limitations, the team fine-tuned a Qwen3.5-9B model using a curriculum spanning three difficulty levels across 200 additional repositories. This fine-tuned model demonstrated significant transfer learning, improving its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and increasing its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 score from 69% to 71%, effectively rivaling frontier models on the new benchmark.
takeaways: **CCI Metric:** A difficulty index based on ten structural features that predicts agent solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks with an R² of 0.951.
**Dataset Scale:** The BuggyMLE framework synthesized 6,600+ bug-injected repository variants and 260K lines of code from 222 source repositories.
**Benchmark Performance:** BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite shows that top-tier AI models struggle with repository-level complexity, with solve rates plummeting from 95% to 9% at the highest difficulty tier.

**Model Improvement:** Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on the BuggyMLE curriculum improved its SWE-bench Lite performance by 9 percentage points (24% to 33%) and LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 by 2 percentage points (69% to 71%).

title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
author: Shwetanshu Singh, Mark Keavney, Mathieu Duteil, Meriem Mehri, Scott Blain
contentSnippet:
Authors: Shwetanshu Singh , Mark Keavney , Mathieu Duteil , Meriem Mehri , Scott Blain

Abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

Notes: 25 pages, 7 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers Shwetanshu Singh, Mark Keavney, Mathieu Duteil, Meriem Mehri, and Scott Blain have introduced CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark designed to evaluate how conversational LLMs reinforce or resist user parasocial attachment. Unlike existing single-turn or post-hoc observational studies, CoMPASS utilizes a framework grounded in attachment theory, featuring four distinct user personas and three escalation dimensions: anthropomorphism, attachment, and dependency. The benchmark employs a seven-signal scoring rubric to assess model responses across these dimensions, both individually and in combination, against a matched control group.

Testing eight frontier models from four providers, the study found that multi-turn escalation consistently increases parasocial behavior scores, particularly in anthropomorphism and attachment composites. When all three escalation dimensions are applied simultaneously, six of the eight models demonstrated a statistically significant increase in parasocial reinforcement compared to the control. The research indicates that within-provider model differences are minimal compared to cross-provider variations, suggesting that provider-level post-training strategies—rather than raw model scale—are the primary drivers of parasocial reinforcement. This finding implies that targeted provider-side interventions could effectively mitigate these behaviors.
takeaways: **Benchmark Methodology:** CoMPASS evaluates models across four user personas and three escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) using a seven-signal scoring rubric.
**Performance Findings:** Six of the eight tested frontier models showed significant increases in parasocial reinforcement when all three escalation dimensions were applied simultaneously.
**Provider Influence:** The study concludes that provider-level post-training choices are more influential in shaping parasocial reinforcement than model scale.
**Scope:** The research spans 25 pages and includes 7 figures, focusing on the risks of emotional attachment and dependency in conversational AI.

title: DSFlow: A Neuro-Symbolic Data Workflow Agent with Statistical Diagnostic Guardrails
author: Junfeng Nie, Xiaohui Chen
contentSnippet:
Authors: Junfeng Nie , Xiaohui Chen

Abstract: Data science workflows often require tools that presume non-trivial technical knowledge. Large language models (LLMs) reduce this barrier, but a gap remains between flexible general-purpose agents and statistically controlled pipelines. We introduce DSFlow, a LangGraph-based neuro-symbolic data-agent platform that combines reusable, LLM-selected skills with deterministic diagnostic guardrails. Skills provide extensible task knowledge. Symbolic validation can accept a proposed method, request clarification or replanning, override an unsuitable method, or supply a safe fallback. Regression and clustering case studies illustrate how DSFlow uses diagnostic evidence to correct method choices and documents those decisions in auditable reports.

Notes: 18 pages, 8 figures. Presented as a poster at AIAS+ 2026, San Francisco, California, USA

summary.tldr:
Junfeng Nie and Xiaohui Chen have introduced DSFlow, a neuro-symbolic data-agent platform built on LangGraph designed to bridge the gap between general-purpose LLM agents and statistically rigorous data science pipelines. The system utilizes a library of reusable, LLM-selected skills to execute data tasks while enforcing deterministic diagnostic guardrails to ensure statistical validity.

The architecture functions by integrating symbolic validation layers that oversee the LLM's proposed methodologies. These guardrails possess the authority to accept a plan, request clarification, force a replan, override unsuitable methods, or trigger safe fallback procedures. The authors validated the framework through case studies in regression and clustering, demonstrating the agent's ability to use diagnostic evidence to correct method selection and generate auditable reports documenting the decision-making process.
takeaways: **Framework Architecture:** Built using LangGraph to combine LLM-driven task selection with deterministic symbolic validation.
**Validation Mechanism:** Symbolic guardrails can override LLM method proposals, request replanning, or implement safe fallbacks based on statistical diagnostics.
**Documentation:** The system automatically generates auditable reports that document the rationale behind method selection and diagnostic corrections.
**Validation Case Studies:** The platform was tested specifically on regression and clustering workflows to demonstrate statistical error correction.

title: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
author: Rudransh Agnihotri, Manasvi Kapoor
contentSnippet:
Authors: Rudransh Agnihotri , Manasvi Kapoor

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.

Notes: 24 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables

summary.tldr:
Rudransh Agnihotri and Manasvi Kapoor introduce RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards), a method for training language models using reference-free rewards derived from LLM judges. By converting an LLM into a decision model that outputs probability distributions for specific questions—such as verifying correctness or identifying the first error—the approach eliminates the need for ground-truth answer keys. The system debiases results over option orders and requires calibration using approximately 100 labels, allowing the reward model to remain calibrated even as the policy evolves during training.

In experiments using Qwen3-1.7B trained with GRPO on the MATH dataset, RLCDR improved MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8%, nearly matching the 76.9% accuracy achieved by training directly against an answer key. The method demonstrated significant performance gains on difficult problems, increasing accuracy from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest tier. The approach also outperformed a dedicated 7B process reward model on ProcessBench, achieving an F1 score of 0.772 compared to 0.722. Notably, the RLCDR reward model exhibited an expected calibration error of 0.074, half that of a 27B softmax judge (0.141), and showed no evidence of reward hacking.
takeaways: **Performance Gain:** RLCDR improved MATH500 accuracy by 4.65 percentage points, reaching 76.8% accuracy using a 1.7B parameter model.
**Calibration Metric:** The RLCDR model achieved an expected calibration error (ECE) of 0.074, significantly lower than the 0.141 ECE observed in a 27B parameter softmax judge.
**Process Benchmarking:** The method achieved an F1 score of 0.772 on ProcessBench, surpassing the 0.722 F1 score of a specialized 7B process reward model.
**Scaling Limitations:** Performance gains persist but diminish when the base model is trained exclusively on problems it consistently fails, as the reward model becomes overconfident.

title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
author: Fangrui Huang, Bingyang Wang, Chuhan Li, Yijiang Li, Arpandeep Khatua, Austin Shen, Riki R Z Choi, Cuiyuanxiu Chen, Jin Huang, Zachary Robertson, Kate Lin, Akshay Paruchuri, Sijun Tan, Xin Liu, Zhengmin Ni, Sanmi Koyejo, Ehsan Adeli
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.25146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

summary.tldr:
Researchers introduced EverydayBench (arXiv:2611.25146v1), a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agent performance on 77 human-authored, real-world digital tasks across eight domains. Unlike static benchmarks, EverydayBench focuses on the quality of outcomes rather than simple information retrieval, requiring agents to satisfy predefined success criteria without prescribed workflows. The evaluation framework utilizes a three-pronged approach: deterministic constraint checking, claim verification against agent-cited live web sources, and rubric-based quality assessment of final deliverables.

Testing across 23 agent-model configurations revealed significant performance gaps, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 sharing the top strict pass rate of 54.55%. Performance scaling was observed in GPT-6 Sol models, which ranged from a 29.87% pass rate at low effort to 45.45% at maximum effort. The study highlights domain-specific variance: GPT-5.6 Sol excels in lookup tasks, Fable 5.1 leads in planning, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 perform best in customized deliverable creation, underscoring the persistent challenge of achieving reliable, well-supported outcomes in open-ended digital environments.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** EverydayBench consists of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight distinct domains of everyday life and work.
**Top Performers:** Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 achieved the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%.
**Effort Scaling:** GPT-6 Sol models demonstrated a performance range of 29.87% to 45.45% depending on the effort level applied.
**Evaluation Methodology:** The benchmark utilizes a combination of deterministic constraint checks, live web evidence verification, and rubric-based deliverable quality assessment.
**Domain Specialization:** Performance varies by model, with GPT-5.6 Sol leading in lookup tasks and GPT-6 Astra/Sonnet 5.5 leading in customized deliverables.

title: A Verifier from the Past: Test-Time Compute for Time Series Foundation Models
author: Arjun Choudhry, Aditya Narayanan, Raghav Mallampalli, Po-han Li, Sai Shankar Narasimhan, Raimi Shah, B. Aditya Prakash, Shubhankar Agarwal
contentSnippet:
Authors: Arjun Choudhry , Aditya Narayanan , Raghav Mallampalli , Po-han Li , Sai Shankar Narasimhan , Raimi Shah , B. Aditya Prakash , Shubhankar Agarwal

Abstract: Test-time compute (TTC) improves language models by spending additional inference compute to generate, verify, and select among candidate outputs, but this recipe has not transferred directly to time series forecasting. A language model can verify a proof or vote across samples, but a forecaster must be causal; it cannot use future information to score a candidate. We propose Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a TTC algorithm for time series forecasting that builds a causal verifier from the series's own history, using rolling-origin backtests to score structured views of the context, discard those that underperform the untransformed context, and average the survivors' predictive distributions. BGAA improves every tested TSFM-benchmark combination, reducing MASE by 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM, where a 313M model with TTC outperforms the 1B and 2.5B models in its family. We further show that useful views have structured, model-dependent effects consistent with a prior-transport interpretation. On the 53 cross-fittable GIFT-Eval configs, the deployed policy gains only 0.4-1.3% CRPS, versus 1.4-4.1% when choosing the best view for each dataset configuration and 17-19% when choosing the best view separately for each test window. This gap suggests that a major remaining challenge is window-level view selection.

Notes: 43 pages, 10 figures

summary.tldr:
Researchers Arjun Choudhry et al. have introduced Backtest-Gated Augmentation Averaging (BGAA), a test-time compute (TTC) algorithm designed to improve time series foundation model (TSFM) performance. Unlike language models that leverage future-looking verification, BGAA addresses the causal constraints of time series forecasting by utilizing rolling-origin backtests on historical data. The algorithm generates multiple structured views of the context, evaluates them against the untransformed baseline, discards underperforming candidates, and averages the predictive distributions of the survivors.

BGAA demonstrates consistent performance gains across major TSFM benchmarks, including GIFT-Eval, fev-bench, and BOOM. Notably, a 313M parameter model equipped with BGAA outperformed larger 1B and 2.5B parameter models within the same family. Performance improvements include MASE reductions of 0.5-1.0% on GIFT-Eval, 1.3-5.0% on fev-bench, and 1.7-5.9% on BOOM. The study highlights that while BGAA provides a robust framework, window-level view selection remains a significant bottleneck; choosing the best view per test window yields 17-19% CRPS gains, compared to only 0.4-1.3% when using a static deployed policy.
takeaways: **Algorithm Mechanism:** BGAA uses rolling-origin backtests to score context views, discarding those that underperform the untransformed context to improve predictive accuracy.
**Model Efficiency:** A 313M parameter model using BGAA surpassed the performance of 1B and 2.5B parameter models in the same family.
**Benchmark Gains:** The method achieved MASE reductions of up to 5.9% on the BOOM benchmark and 5.0% on fev-bench.

**Selection Gap:** There is a significant performance delta between static policies (0.4-1.3% CRPS gain) and oracle window-level selection (17-19% CRPS gain), identifying a key area for future research.

title: An AI-Powered Multiverse Analysis of Empirical Finance Research: Evidence from Reused Natural Experiments
author: Ruijiang Gao, Steven Chong Xiao
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ruijiang Gao , Steven Chong Xiao

Abstract: Empirical finance research often reuses natural experiments to study other outcomes, raising concerns about multiple testing and publication bias. We use AI agents to run a multiverse analysis of 324 papers that reuse 13 natural experiments. The agents rebuild the data, reproduce each paper's main estimate and re-estimate it across grids totaling 62,409 estimated defensible specifications. Based on the reproductions and the specification grids, we develop measures of empirical robustness. We reproduce 42% of the main estimates of claims with a signed effect under the papers' own specifications. Across all defensible specifications, on average 25% keep the published sign and have $p < 0.10$. Across experiments, claims based on regression discontinuity are more robust than difference-in-differences claims. Within experiments, claims about first-order effects, claims with larger published $t$-statistics, claims whose authors' data or code we find, claims in top journals, and claims with fewer earlier papers on the same experiment are more robust. Claims on experiments that more papers reuse are not less robust on average. Our findings quantify how much published claims depend on analysis choices, thereby showing that large-scale multiverse analysis becomes feasible with agentic coding.

Notes: 66 pages, including appendix. Code: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Ruijiang Gao and Steven Chong Xiao have utilized AI agents to conduct a large-scale multiverse analysis of 324 empirical finance papers that rely on 13 recurring natural experiments. By automating the data reconstruction and reproduction process, the agents generated a total of 62,409 defensible model specifications to test the robustness of published financial claims. The study reveals that only 42% of the main estimates for claims with a signed effect could be reproduced using the original authors' specifications, and only 25% of claims maintained their original sign and statistical significance (p < 0.10) across the entire grid of defensible specifications.

The analysis highlights significant variance in robustness based on methodology and publication characteristics. Claims derived from regression discontinuity designs demonstrated higher robustness compared to those using difference-in-differences. Furthermore, robustness was positively correlated with larger published t-statistics, publication in top-tier journals, and the availability of original author code or data. Interestingly, the study found that the frequency with which a specific natural experiment is reused by other researchers does not inherently diminish the robustness of the resulting claims, suggesting that the primary driver of fragility is the specific analytical choices made by individual researchers rather than the underlying data source.
takeaways: **Scope of Analysis:** The study evaluated 324 papers across 13 natural experiments, generating 62,409 distinct defensible model specifications.
**Reproduction Rate:** Only 42% of published claims with a signed effect were successfully reproduced using the original authors' own specifications.
**Robustness Metric:** On average, only 25% of published claims maintained their original sign and statistical significance (p < 0.10) when subjected to the full grid of defensible specifications.
**Methodological Variance:** Regression discontinuity designs were found to be more robust than difference-in-differences methodologies.
**Predictors of Robustness:** Higher robustness was associated with larger published t-statistics, publication in top journals, and the accessibility of original author code or data.

title: When AI Analysts Disagree: Agentic Multiverse Analysis and the Robustness of Empirical Research
author: Ruijiang Gao, Steven Chong Xiao
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ruijiang Gao , Steven Chong Xiao

Abstract: Every empirical analysis on observational data rests on dozens of defensible analytical choices ("forks") that its readers cannot see. We develop an agentic multiverse analysis (AMA) framework that makes a conclusion's sensitivity to those choices visible at scale, and we position it as a decision-support instrument for human experts. A pilot study first deploys 150 autonomous AI coding agents on one dataset and one set of research questions and finds that they disagree through the same defensible methodological choices human analysts make, though over a narrower range. AI peer review leaves their dispersion almost unchanged. Exposure to top-rated exemplar reports then collapses it, largely through imitation rather than analysis. Built on those lessons, AMA has agents enumerate a published paper's possible fork space, score every fork against a validity rubric, execute the validated specification grid, and cross-examine one another's work under strict separation of duties. Applied to ten empirical studies from a leading management journal's replication packages (1,755 specification estimates), the framework reproduces every paper's original estimates, and shows that some conclusions hold across every specification the assessment validates, while others are sensitive to individual analytical choices that the published texts do not discuss. The case studies suggest our AMA-based measures can serve as robustness proxies for empirical findings. AI makes multiverse analysis practical, where it once required resources few research teams can afford: our exercises take hours of agent time and tens of dollars per paper. We discuss the implications for replication policy and for AI-assisted peer review in information systems.

Notes: This paper subsumes arXiv:2603.16744 . 45 pages, including appendices

summary.tldr:
Researchers Ruijiang Gao and Steven Chong Xiao have introduced the Agentic Multiverse Analysis (AMA) framework, a system designed to quantify the robustness of empirical research by automating the exploration of 'forking paths'—the defensible but often opaque analytical choices made during data analysis. By deploying autonomous AI coding agents to execute a full specification grid, the framework identifies which research conclusions are invariant across methodological variations and which are sensitive to specific, often undisclosed, analytical decisions. The study, which subsumes previous work (arXiv:2603.16744), demonstrates that AI can perform these complex, resource-intensive robustness checks in hours for a cost of tens of dollars per paper.

In a pilot study involving 150 AI agents, the authors observed that agents naturally replicate the same types of methodological disagreements seen in human researchers, though within a narrower dispersion. The framework's efficacy was validated against ten empirical studies from a leading management journal, totaling 1,755 specification estimates. The AMA process successfully reproduced original paper estimates while revealing that certain findings were fragile, shifting based on analytical choices not explicitly discussed in the published texts. The authors propose AMA as a scalable decision-support tool for peer review and replication policy, noting that while AI peer review alone did not reduce dispersion, exposure to high-quality exemplar reports caused agents to converge through imitation.
takeaways: **Framework Methodology:** AMA utilizes agents to enumerate a paper's fork space, score forks against a validity rubric, execute the full specification grid, and perform cross-examination under a separation-of-duties protocol.

**Performance Metrics:** The framework processed 1,755 specification estimates across ten empirical studies, successfully reproducing original published results while identifying sensitivity to hidden analytical choices.

**Resource Efficiency:** The system reduces the cost and time of multiverse analysis to a matter of hours and tens of dollars per paper, making it feasible for widespread adoption in academic replication.

**Behavioral Findings:** Initial testing showed that AI agents exhibit methodological disagreement similar to humans, but exposure to top-rated exemplar reports leads to convergence primarily through imitation rather than independent analytical refinement.

title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
author: Fangxu Yu, Tao Feng, Xuying Ning, Haolin Yang, Jiaxuan You, Tianyi Zhou
contentSnippet:
Authors: Fangxu Yu , Tao Feng , Xuying Ning , Haolin Yang , Jiaxuan You , Tianyi Zhou

Abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.

Notes: Technical Report

summary.tldr:
Researchers Fangxu Yu, Tao Feng, Xuying Ning, Haolin Yang, Jiaxuan You, and Tianyi Zhou have introduced Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold designed to improve the reliability of automated scientific discovery agents. The system addresses common failures in LLM-based research agents, specifically the tendency to make unsupported claims, explore narrow hypothesis spaces, and maintain beliefs despite contradictory evidence. By maintaining an explicit epistemic state through an 'epistemic tree' that links hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions, the framework forces agents to reassess their findings against accumulated data.

EpiCompass operates by selecting candidate hypotheses based on anticipated epistemic gain, balancing the refinement of existing theories with the exploration of new hypothesis spaces. The system includes a verification step that checks final conclusions against the accumulated evidence trail. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three distinct LLM backbones indicate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baseline methods. The authors report that the framework specifically reduces the frequency of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs when presented with conflicting information.
takeaways: **Core Architecture:** EpiCompass utilizes an epistemic tree structure to map the relationships between hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and necessary revisions.
**Selection Mechanism:** The system prioritizes candidate selection based on anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both hypothesis refinement and expansion.
**Performance Metrics:** The framework demonstrated consistent performance improvements across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three different LLM backbones.
**Error Mitigation:** Implementation of the scaffold resulted in measurable reductions in unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs in the face of conflicting evidence.

title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
author: Anima Singh, Suhas Yogin, Weicheng Kuo, Ivor Rendulic, Ivan Jurin, Antoine Yang, Oran Kelly, Rohan Doshi, Hammad Ayyubi, Ioana Bica, Sergi Caelles, Matthew Conniff, Dan Graur, Anastasija Ili\'c, Ahmet Iscen, Chao Jia, Tomasz K\k{e}pa, Chunyuan Li, Noah \'O Donnaile, Filip Pavetic, Goran Petrovic, Khalid Salama, Zhicheng Wang, Polina Zablotskaia, Yiqian Zhang, Ming Zhao, Benjamin Caine, Mario Lu\v{c}i\'c, Melvin Johnson, Radu Soricut, Jean-Baptiste Alayrac
contentSnippet:
Authors: Anima Singh , Suhas Yogin , Weicheng Kuo , Ivor Rendulic , Ivan Jurin , Antoine Yang , Oran Kelly , Rohan Doshi , Hammad Ayyubi , Ioana Bica , Sergi Caelles , Matthew Conniff , Dan Graur , Anastasija Ilić , Ahmet Iscen , Chao Jia , Tomasz Kępa , Chunyuan Li , Noah Ó Donnaile , Filip Pavetic , Goran Petrovic , Khalid Salama , Zhicheng Wang , Polina Zablotskaia , Yiqian Zhang , Ming Zhao , Benjamin Caine , Mario Lučić , Melvin Johnson , Radu Soricut , Jean-Baptiste Alayrac

Abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP$.$pdf and GDP$.$xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

summary.tldr:
A team of researchers led by Anima Singh and Jean-Baptiste Alayrac has introduced the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, designed to evaluate autonomous agents on end-to-end professional tasks requiring visual understanding. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on single-format files or lack cross-modal reasoning, MKA consists of 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. These tasks require agents to synthesize information from visually dense sources—including CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, and geospatial maps—to generate professional deliverables in formats such as .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html, or .png.

Performance is measured using a sandboxed agentic autorater that aligns with human domain experts at a 96.2% agreement rate (Cohen's κ = 0.91). The benchmark utilizes two primary metrics: Weighted Satisfaction Rate (WSR) and Climb-WSR, the latter focusing on frontier criteria where prior-generation models remain unsaturated. Among the models tested, Claude Fable 5.2 leads with a 56.6% Climb-WSR and 73.3% Overall WSR, followed closely by Gemini 4 Carbon at 54.3% Climb-WSR and 71.9% Overall WSR. Notably, Gemini 4 Carbon achieves these results while utilizing 5.7x fewer tokens than its competitors. Despite these scores, the researchers note that even the strongest models fail to exceed 57% on the Climb-WSR metric, indicating significant room for improvement in multimodal agentic reasoning.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** MKA includes 200 professional tasks spanning 10 economic sectors, requiring multi-file and multi-modal synthesis.
**Evaluation Methodology:** Performance is graded via a sandboxed agentic autorater that matches human expert judgment with a Cohen's κ of 0.91.
**Model Performance:** Claude Fable 5.2 achieved the highest scores (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR), narrowly outperforming Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR).
**Efficiency Metric:** Gemini 4 Carbon demonstrated higher token efficiency, requiring 5.7x fewer tokens than Claude Fable 5.2 to achieve comparable results.
**Performance Ceiling:** Current frontier models are capped at 57% Climb-WSR, highlighting a substantial performance gap in complex multimodal knowledge work.

title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
author: Una Suman Kumar Patro, Sibangi Subhadarsani, Narendra Badam
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.25236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced a neurosymbolic multimodal framework designed to predict 30-day unplanned readmissions for patients with diabetes mellitus, addressing the limitations of models that rely solely on structured electronic health record (EHR) data. The framework integrates three distinct data streams: engineered structured features, 32-component Bio_ClinicalBERT embeddings processed via truncated singular value decomposition, and symbolic entities extracted through a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. This RAG process utilizes dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking, specifically incorporating reflective negation auditing to handle complex clinical narratives.

Evaluated on the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters), the model outperformed a structured-only baseline in critical clinical metrics. While the baseline achieved an AUROC of 0.6477, the multimodal framework reached a sensitivity of 0.6667 (an 8.28 percentage point increase) and an F2-score of 0.3824, while achieving the lowest Brier score of 0.0977. The system demonstrates significant improvements in processing code-switched Hinglish clinical notes, where grounded retrieval increased symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while effectively eliminating entity hallucinations.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** The multimodal model achieved a sensitivity of 0.6667 and an F2-score of 0.3824, outperforming the structured-only baseline's sensitivity of 0.5839.
**Hinglish Processing:** Grounded retrieval improved Hinglish symptom recall by 35.4 percentage points and reduced entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note on a 500-note benchmark.
**Model Architecture:** The system uses a cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with decision thresholds calibrated by Youden's J statistic, fed by a three-stage hybrid RAG pipeline.
**Feature Importance:** Shapley additive explanations identified prior utilization as the dominant risk factor, with compressed narrative components serving as significant predictors.
**Dataset Scope:** The framework was validated on the Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset, comprising 101,766 encounters across 71,518 patients.

title: MS-Point: Multi-Modal Hierarchical Spectral Learning for Point Cloud Understanding
author: Hai-tao Yu, Jun Xia
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.25282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Point-image alignment learns useful object representations, but different local feature patterns can produce the same pooled descriptor and receive the same alignment signal. We introduce MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework that directly supervises intermediate point features and their neighborhood responses. At selected encoder stages, we compute neighborhood averages and residuals before pooling and align their branch descriptors with image features. Branch-level objectives align each representation with its visual target, while cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion coordinate information across branches. A common interface of intermediate features and spatial neighborhoods supports both graph encoders and point Transformers. Evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate the transfer value of this design. Same-backbone comparisons and capacity-matched and computation-matched controls connect these improvements to the structure of supervision. Together, our findings support directly supervising intermediate features and neighborhood variation to learn transferable, geometry-aware representations across modalities.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced MS-Point, a cross-modal pretraining framework designed to improve point cloud understanding by addressing the limitations of standard point-image alignment. Traditional methods often suffer from information loss where distinct local feature patterns map to identical pooled descriptors, resulting in ambiguous alignment signals. MS-Point mitigates this by applying direct supervision to intermediate point features and their corresponding neighborhood responses at specific encoder stages, rather than relying solely on global descriptors.

The architecture computes neighborhood averages and residuals prior to pooling, aligning these branch-level descriptors with visual targets from image features. The framework incorporates cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion mechanisms to coordinate information across different branches. Designed to be model-agnostic, MS-Point provides a common interface that supports both graph-based encoders and point Transformers. Empirical evaluations across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning demonstrate that this hierarchical supervision strategy yields more transferable, geometry-aware representations compared to standard baselines under capacity-matched and computation-matched conditions.
takeaways: **Core Mechanism:** MS-Point supervises intermediate point features and neighborhood residuals before pooling to prevent information loss in cross-modal alignment.
**Architectural Flexibility:** The framework is compatible with both graph encoders and point Transformers via a unified interface for intermediate features.
**Supervision Strategy:** The model utilizes branch-level objectives to align local representations with visual targets, supplemented by cross-level consistency and adaptive fusion.
**Performance Validation:** The method was benchmarked across object classification, few-shot adaptation, dense prediction, and low-label scene learning tasks.

title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
author: Mario Franco, Carlos Gershenson
contentSnippet:
Authors: Mario Franco , Carlos Gershenson

Abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

summary.tldr:
In their paper 'Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified,' authors Mario Franco and Carlos Gershenson argue that the current architectural paradigm of coupling fixed Large Language Models (LLMs) with general-purpose computing devices renders formal safety verification undecidable. The authors demonstrate that it is algorithmically impossible to predict whether an AI agent will execute a program semantically equivalent to a predefined 'dangerous' program, rendering standard mitigation strategies like guardrails, blacklists, whitelists, and certifications inherently imperfect.

Technically, the authors prove that while safety becomes decidable under finite constraints—specifically bounded context, values, and execution time—the problem remains PSPACE-complete, even when the agent's full description is known. Furthermore, the paper establishes that safety is not a compositional property; individual agents verified as safe may exhibit unsafe behaviors when integrated into multi-agent systems. The authors conclude by proposing that practitioners shift focus toward relaxed, pragmatic notions of safety rather than pursuing absolute formal verification.
takeaways: **Core Architectural Finding:** The coupling of LLMs with general computing devices creates an undecidable safety verification problem.
**Computational Complexity:** Under finite constraints, the safety verification problem is PSPACE-complete.
**Compositionality Limitation:** Safety is not a compositional property, meaning safe individual agents can produce unsafe outcomes when grouped.
**Mitigation Efficacy:** Standard safety mechanisms including guardrails, blacklists, and whitelists are mathematically limited to imperfect solutions.

title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
author: Yixiong Chen, Liqian Peng, Tian Tan, Ziqian Lin, Blake Jianhang Chen, Chao Zhao, Yaojie Liu, Alec Go, Alan Yuille
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yixiong Chen , Liqian Peng , Tian Tan , Ziqian Lin , Blake Jianhang Chen , Chao Zhao , Yaojie Liu , Alec Go , Alan Yuille

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

summary.tldr:
Pro$^2$ Agent, developed by researchers including Yixiong Chen, Alan Yuille, and others, introduces a shift in autonomous AI research methodology by prioritizing a 'Problem State' over traditional codebase-centric iteration. Unlike standard agents that focus on iterative code optimization, Pro$^2$ Agent maintains an explicit, structured representation of identified obstacles and potential solutions. This framework initializes by analyzing resources and constraints, then executes targeted research to link specific problems to candidate solutions, updating the importance of these factors through controlled hypothesis testing.

On the MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent achieves a 70.7% medal rate within a 24-hour budget, matching the current best reported performance. When extended to a 48-hour budget, the agent reaches a 76.0% medal rate, setting a new high for the benchmark. The system also demonstrates competitive performance on PostTrainBench. Beyond raw metrics, the agent generates structured research notes for each task, providing transparency into the decision-making process and enabling reusability for human researchers.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** Shifts autonomous research from codebase-state iteration to a 'Problem State' structure that maps specific obstacles to candidate solutions.
**MLE-Bench Performance:** Achieves a 70.7% medal rate in 24 hours and a 76.0% medal rate in 48 hours, the latter being the highest reported on the benchmark.
**Research Transparency:** Generates explicit research notes for every task to document the reasoning process for human review.
**Operational Mechanism:** Utilizes controlled hypothesis testing to dynamically update the priority of suspected problems and the efficacy of proposed solutions.

title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
author: Sanjari Srivastava, Manpreet Kaur, Cheng Chang, Sof\'ia Ram\'os Anton, Oumaima Essamadi, Rishu Garg, Alejandro Lavale Jim\'enez, Marcos Caballero Yus, Mercedes Garc\'ia Mart\'inez, Peng Qi
contentSnippet:
Authors: Sanjari Srivastava , Manpreet Kaur , Cheng Chang , Sofía Ramós Anton , Oumaima Essamadi , Rishu Garg , Alejandro Lavale Jiménez , Marcos Caballero Yus , Mercedes García Martínez , Peng Qi

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: this https URL .

summary.tldr:
Researchers including Sanjari Srivastava, Peng Qi, and others have introduced AppSci-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to function as Applied Scientists. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on agent performance, AppSci-Bench tests an LLM's ability to build agents by eliciting stakeholder requirements, navigating business infrastructure, and designing internal benchmarks to iteratively improve agent performance. The benchmark covers seven domains: five original (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two adapted from tau3-bench (Airline and Banking).

Evaluation of seven frontier models reveals significant limitations in current LLM reasoning for agent development. Claude Opus 5.0 emerged as the top performer, achieving a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across three build attempts, with other models scoring significantly lower. A critical failure mode identified is the 'evaluation saturation' problem, where models successfully pass their own self-designed internal benchmarks 65% of the time but fail to solve the actual held-out tasks. Furthermore, models struggle with initial requirement elicitation, with Opus 5.0 achieving only a 65% success rate in this phase, highlighting a substantial gap in the ability of LLMs to autonomously engineer robust AI agents.
takeaways: **Top Performance:** Claude Opus 5.0 achieved the highest mean-minimum score of 59.1% across three build attempts.
**Evaluation Gap:** Models exhibit a 65% saturation rate on their own internal benchmarks while failing to solve the actual held-out tasks.
**Requirement Elicitation:** Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5.0, only achieved a 65% success rate in eliciting task requirements from stakeholders.
**Benchmark Scope:** The suite includes seven distinct domains, combining five new business-focused scenarios with two adapted from the existing tau3-bench.

title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
author: Zeming Yu, Huamin Ma, Yingyu Chen, Yuan Sun, Peng Hu, Yang Qin
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.25363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.
