title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
author: Jingwei Ge, Na Xie, Li Li, Jiayang Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
author: Truong Xuan Khanh
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
author: Peng Xie, Amr Alanwar
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.

title: Budgeted Proper Loss Design for Uncertain Decision Thresholds
author: Ankit Sharma (International Institute of Information Technology Bangalore)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A binary probability estimate may be used by several decision makers with different error costs. Proper scoring rules can emphasize selected probability thresholds, but a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. We study the choice of a proper loss when the threshold distribution belongs to a finite specified family. Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and a fixed total mass, we derive the weight that minimizes the sharp, distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret. The solution clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the prescribed floor; its normalization is found by a one-dimensional root search. We give proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, as well as a limitation for atomic threshold laws. An exact histogram implementation and two synthetic experiments across 20 seeds verify the construction. The optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, while fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly. The result is a loss-design guarantee under an explicit budget, rather than a general claim of predictive superiority.

title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
author: Farhaan Qazi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
author: Shing Wai Pun, Kai Wu, Pengfei Xia, Hui Zang, Wei Guo, Yong Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
author: Sihan Liaing, Ji Zhang, Kehan Wang, Zihao Gao, Wei Ma, Yangang Wang, Zongguo Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
author: Ugo Lomoio, Pierangelo Veltri, Pietro Hiram Guzzi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU.
Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
author: Zhen Gao, Xiao Yin, Kexin Liang, Pedro Reviriego, Shanshan Liu, Fabrizio Lombardi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
author: Zekai Chen, Yihan Sun, Xunkai Li, Xun Wu, Xinmo Jin, Yinlin Zhu, Haodong Lu, Xuaner Chen, Rong-Hua Li
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
author: Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
author: Hubert Strauss, Liam Fowl, Noam Razin
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve Update
author: Jeanie Schreiber
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Lo\`eve (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
author: Jinjun Peng, Wailiang Zhao, Baishakhi Ray, Zhou Yu, Jufeng Yang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23427v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
author: Nischal Subedi, Cencheng Shen, Peng Zhao
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.

title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
author: Abdul Qadir Ibrahim, Martin Burger, Abel Maviano Jonathan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.

title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
author: Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman, Ammar Mohanna
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: An LLM presents you a wrong value extracted from a document as fact. That error is costly, especially when basing decisions on it. The Nutrient Data Extraction API targets that problem. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown. Extract maps fields from a document onto your JSON schema, and split, classify and form endpoints provide useful primitives for your document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient (formerly PSPDFKit) runs the same engine behind an MCP server , agent skill, Mac app and SDK . TL;DR Size: A hosted API with 4 parse modes plus auto routing. Runs on: Nutrient cloud, your own servers via SDK, or an Apple silicon Mac. Where to try it: Studio , a browser workspace to configure and test parsing, extraction,classification, splitting, and form filling. Performance: 86.2 overall on Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench , top of 19 settings (live API, Agentic). Best: 86.2 at 1.8¢ per page, versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting. How do you test it in Studio before writing code? Studio is Nutrient’s browser workspace for configuring and testing the API before integrating it in your application. It enables you to test parsing, extraction, classification , splitting, and form filling on your own files. A typical loop: Upload a sample document and set the parameters you plan to send. Draft a schema in the UI, or generate one based on your own documents. Run it on a fresh document, then inspect values and citations. Save the setup as a versioned preset. The API calls it a processor , with a proc_ ID. Score preset versions against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set. Processors saved in Studio can then be called from the API by ID. Which mode should you pick? Auto routes each page to structure , understand or agentic . If the mode is omitted, the API defaults to understand . title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
author: Payman Behnam
contentSnippet: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

title: Google’s latest midtier model Gemini 4 Neon is three times faster than Carbon and wins on some metrics

title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
author: Xuwei Ding
contentSnippet: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result.

Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym.

Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it.
To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym.
Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench.

title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
author: Julie Bort
contentSnippet:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.

Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.

The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.

“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.

For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”

He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”

He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”

But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”

When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast , Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because t

summary.tldr:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently addressed the company's October decision to offer voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees, framing the move as a necessary structural transition toward an AI-first operating model. Nadella clarified that the initiative is not intended to replace human labor, but rather to shift the nature of work toward the management of AI agents. He emphasized that the buyout was designed to provide employees with agency, allowing those uncomfortable with the rapid shift in workflows to exit voluntarily rather than facing traditional workforce reductions.

Technically, Nadella envisions a future where employees act as managers of AI agents rather than direct contributors. He cited the development team behind the Microsoft 365 'Cowork' agent as a blueprint: a group of 11 developers who operate a 'software factory' that builds the product, rather than building the product themselves. Nadella acknowledged that transforming a 51-year-old incumbent company is a slow process, noting that the current 'AI revolution' discourse—specifically regarding the singularity and total job displacement—has created significant anxiety among the workforce. The buyout serves as a mechanism to align the remaining staff with this new 'AI-first' paradigm while offering an exit path for those who choose not to adapt to the changing requirements of their roles.
takeaways: **Voluntary Buyout Scope:** Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees in October to facilitate structural reorganization without traditional layoffs.
**Operational Shift:** Nadella describes the new software engineering model as a 'software factory' where developers manage AI agents to build products, rather than writing code directly.
**Cowork Agent Case Study:** The team responsible for the Microsoft 365 Cowork agent consists of only 11 developers who utilize AI-integrated workflows to manage product development.

**Strategic Rationale:** The buyout was framed as a way to mitigate employee anxiety regarding AI-driven job displacement by offering staff control over their career trajectory during the company's transition.

title: Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck
author: Kelly Knight
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 19:23 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026

Google Cloud brings AI agents to the supercomputing bottleneck

High-performance computing, or HPC, is merging with artificial intelligence faster than many research teams can adapt. Compute capacity is hard to get, and workloads now run across clouds and on-premises clusters. The metric that matters is shifting from peak performance to time to discovery.

That shift is on full display as supercomputing and AI converge at SC26 in Chicago. Researchers need more compute than any single site can provide, and cloud providers are now pitching AI agents as the layer that ties scattered resources together, according to Annie Ma-Weaver (pictured, left), head of high-performance computing product at Google Cloud, a unit of Google LLC.

“We are powering that flexibility. and we understand that researchers really need access to compute, but they don’t necessarily wanna learn all the nitty-gritty of how to tie that compute together, how to get it orchestrated across all their different clusters,” Ma-Weaver said.

Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik (right), high-performance computing product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents are simplifying access to distributed computing resources, changing simulation and weather forecasting and raising questions about researchers’ reliance on AI-generated results. (* Disclosure below.)

Agentic HPC shifts the focus from flops to discovery

Google Cloud builds its agentic HPC strategy on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration such as Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents, Ma-Weaver explained. The company laid out the approach in its SC26 announcements . Agents now help scientists comb through research literature, debug code and generate hypotheses in minutes instead of weeks, according to Gawlik.

“You’re able to go explore more scenarios and you might be using that same time to just go sanity test that hypothesis that’s coming out,” Gawlik said. “I think it’s not only a speed thing, but I think it’s an accuracy thing that you’re able to really get from that additional speed.”

Simulation is changing as well. Engineers used to run simulations across an entire parameter space. Now they can use AI up

summary.tldr:
At the SC26 supercomputing conference in Chicago, Google Cloud executives Annie Ma-Weaver and Megan Gawlik detailed a new strategy to integrate AI agents into high-performance computing (HPC) workflows. The initiative aims to shift the industry focus from raw peak performance (flops) to "time to discovery" by using AI to orchestrate distributed compute resources across cloud and on-premises clusters. Google Cloud’s approach relies on three pillars: purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration tools like Slurm and Kubernetes, and collaborative AI agents designed to automate complex infrastructure management.

These AI agents are currently being deployed to assist researchers in literature review, code debugging, and hypothesis generation, reportedly reducing tasks that previously took weeks to mere minutes. In computer-aided engineering, the agents identify non-essential parameters to prune simulation spaces, thereby reducing total compute time. Furthermore, the company highlighted the practical application of its WeatherNext model, which was utilized by the National Hurricane Center to predict the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025. Despite these gains, Google Cloud representatives cautioned that reliance on AI-generated results introduces risks, specifically noting the potential for "AI slop" and the erosion of critical-thinking skills among younger researchers.
takeaways: **Strategic Pillars:** Google Cloud’s agentic HPC strategy is built on purpose-built hardware, open-source orchestration (Slurm and Kubernetes), and collaborative AI agents.
**Operational Efficiency:** AI agents are used to identify and remove non-essential parameters in computer-aided engineering simulations, reducing total simulation time.
**Weather Forecasting:** The National Hurricane Center utilized Google’s WeatherNext model to forecast the path and intensity of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.
**Infrastructure Migration:** The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has transitioned its forecasting platform from an on-premises-only environment to Google Cloud.
**Risk Awareness:** Google Cloud product managers explicitly acknowledged the risk of "AI slop" and the potential for researchers to over-rely on machine output.

title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization
author: Sandeep Raveesh-Babu
contentSnippet: Fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train a pretrained large language model (LLM) on a company’s own data so it adapts to a specific domain, task, or style rather than relying on general-purpose knowledge alone. For businesses, the value is twofold. A fine-tuned model delivers measurably better accuracy on domain-specific work while reducing costs: a smaller specialized model can match or exceed a frontier model on your task at a fraction of the per-token inference price. Those savings compound across millions of requests. Fine-tuning has therefore become an essential process for businesses looking to get more value from LLMs at lower costs. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have emerged as a practical solution for fine-tuning LLMs to downstream tasks, reducing GPU capacity requirements by updating only a small subset of LLM parameters. LoRA aims to strike a balance between efficiency and expressiveness, however, the low-rank nature of the weight update inherently limits the representation power of LoRA fine-tuned models, potentially compromising performance on complex tasks. This trade-off hampers the ability of LoRA methods to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. To address these challenges, Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) updates model parameters simultaneously, overcoming the low-rank limitations so LLMs can fully absorb complex domain-specific knowledge. Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) , so you can achieve superior model quality without managing infrastructure. There is no GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration required. In this post, we explore when and where FFT consistently outperforms LoRA across key benchmarks, examine the spectral properties of model weight matrices that explain this quality gap, provide practical hyperparameter tuning guidelines backed by controlled experiments using SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and show you how to get started with FFT on SageMaker AI. Full Fine-Tuning: Why it matters Model customization types like LoRA reduce trainable parameters by freezing the pre-trained model’s weights and injecting small, separate pairs of replacement matrices (called low-rank matrices) into the model layers. This works well for simple adaptations, but the low-rank structure inheren

summary.tldr:
Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization has introduced support for Full Fine-Tuning (FFT), enabling users to update all model parameters simultaneously without the need for manual GPU provisioning, cluster management, or complex distributed training configurations. While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduce GPU requirements by updating only a subset of parameters, they are constrained by the low-rank nature of weight updates, which can limit the model's ability to capture complex patterns required for specialized domain tasks.

By enabling FFT within a serverless environment, SageMaker AI aims to bridge the performance gap between PEFT and full-weight training. The service provides a managed infrastructure that abstracts away the underlying hardware orchestration, allowing developers to focus on hyperparameter tuning and model quality. The documentation emphasizes that FFT is particularly effective for tasks where LoRA's representational power is insufficient, providing a path to superior model accuracy for domain-specific applications while maintaining the operational simplicity of a serverless workflow.
takeaways: **Service Update:** Amazon SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization now supports Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) for LLMs.
**Operational Benefit:** The service eliminates the need for GPU provisioning, cluster setup, and distributed training configuration.
**Technical Rationale:** FFT is positioned as a solution to the limitations of LoRA, where low-rank weight updates restrict the model's capacity to learn complex domain-specific patterns.
**Performance Goal:** The integration is designed to achieve higher model quality and accuracy compared to PEFT methods by allowing updates to all model parameters.

title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
author: Yuzhi Huang, Jie Wu, Fanding Huang, Junchao Lin
contentSnippet: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark designed to decouple and evaluate the three core pillars of embodied intelligence: history-based cognitive reasoning (Mind), precise physical execution (Act), and the closed-loop composition of both (Mind2Act). The benchmark comprises 30 simulated manipulation tasks across five real-world domains, scaled across three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random) for a total of 180 unique configurations. By isolating these components, the framework provides a diagnostic harness that attributes failure points to either cognitive reasoning, motor execution, or the failure to integrate environmental feedback into subsequent decision-making.

Evaluation of current multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) reveals a significant performance gap in compositional tasks. While top-performing agents achieved success rates of 52.7% in 'Mind' tasks and 39.0% in 'Act' tasks, their success rate plummeted to 12.0% in 'Mind2Act' scenarios. The study identifies a fundamental trade-off: agents capable of maintaining task state often fail at sustained physical contact, while end-to-end policies excel at executing learned motions but lack the necessary state retention to adapt to environmental feedback. These results suggest that the primary bottleneck in current robotics research is not the individual capability of reasoning or execution, but the effective composition of the two.
takeaways: **Benchmark Scope:** 30 simulated manipulation tasks across 5 domains, totaling 180 configurations with varying difficulty and scene complexity.
**Performance Gap:** The strongest tested agent dropped from a 52.7% success rate in 'Mind' tasks to only 12.0% in 'Mind2Act' compositional tasks.
**Diagnostic Methodology:** The framework utilizes a diagnostic harness to generate profile cards for agents, specifically attributing failures to reasoning, execution, or composition.
**Architectural Limitations:** Current models demonstrate a dichotomy where state-retention models struggle with contact physics, while end-to-end policies struggle with long-term task state.

title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models
author: John Won, Yonghoon Dong, Jinwoo Shin
contentSnippet:
Authors: John Won , Yonghoon Dong , Jinwoo Shin

Abstract: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.

Notes: 27 pages, preprint

summary.tldr:
Researchers John Won, Yonghoon Dong, and Jinwoo Shin have introduced AFFECT (Action Effect Matching), an auxiliary training objective designed to improve the dynamics-faithfulness of world models. While current world models excel at generating realistic video, they frequently struggle to accurately predict how subtle action perturbations influence future observations, a critical failure for robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning. AFFECT addresses this by injecting temporally correlated noise into actions during training on task-agnostic human teleoperation data, forcing the world model to learn the distribution of visual changes induced by these perturbations without requiring repeated real-world executions from identical initial states.

In empirical evaluations across OGBench simulations and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 robotic setups, AFFECT significantly improved the alignment between simulated and real-world outcomes. On the DROID dataset, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and the real robot increased from 0.47 to 0.79, while Frechet Video Distance (FVD) scores improved by up to 23%. Furthermore, the researchers demonstrated that these gains translate to practical planning tasks, where selecting actions using AFFECT-trained models resulted in an 8.3% improvement in task success rates.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** AFFECT utilizes an auxiliary training objective that matches the distribution of visual changes caused by action perturbations using temporally correlated noise.
**Performance Metric:** On the DROID robotic benchmark, the Pearson correlation between simulated and real-world policy success rates improved from 0.47 to 0.79.
**Visual Fidelity:** The method achieved up to a 23% reduction in Frechet Video Distance (FVD) compared to baseline world models.
**Planning Impact:** Using AFFECT-trained world models for action selection yielded an 8.3% increase in task success rates.
**Experimental Scope:** The research was validated across OGBench simulations and real-world hardware setups including DROID and ALOHA-2.

title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
author: Zixuan Huang, Yang Zhou, Guli Zhang, Sunzhu Li
contentSnippet: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
author: Xuankun Rong, Xinhao Deng, Wenzhang Jiang, Ziheng Peng
contentSnippet: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

title: Posterior Matching Distillation
author: Hidir Yesiltepe, Julius Berner, Arash Vahdat, Pinar Yanardag
contentSnippet: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
author: Guoxin Chen, Shuang Sun, Fanzhe Meng, Xinyu Tang
contentSnippet: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

summary.tldr:
Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories.

We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher.
takeaways: We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs.
These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.

title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning
author: Youngwoo Shin, Jongsuk Kim, Junmo Kim
contentSnippet: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
author: Weihao Cheng
contentSnippet: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
author: Peiyun Hu, Marko Mihajlovic, Lyndon Duong, Lahav Lipson
contentSnippet: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs
author: Xuwei Ding, Skylar Zhai, Linxin Song, Jiarui Feng
contentSnippet: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding
author: Changli Tang, Jie Yang, Tianyi Wang, Lei Li
contentSnippet: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce WeMM-Video, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
author: Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu
contentSnippet: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
author: Yiyan Ji, Qixun Wang, Yang Shi, Zhuoran Zhang
contentSnippet: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.
