title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
author: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
contentSnippet:
Authors: Amit Feldman , Ilan Shimshoni , Rotem Dror

Abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, and Rotem Dror have introduced a framework for online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric procedural videos. Unlike existing methods that either ignore text instructions or operate exclusively offline, this model processes video streams in real-time to identify action attempts, localize them temporally, and classify execution status as correct, modified, slip, correction, or addition. Omitted steps are identified post-video. The authors repartitioned the EgoPER dataset to include erroneous videos across all splits to facilitate supervised learning for mistake detection.

The study compares a modular pipeline—which separates step identification, temporal localization, and verification—against a joint model that performs all tasks in a single inference step. While both architectures achieved comparable step-segmentation F1@0.5 scores (93.6% for the modular approach vs. 92.1% for the joint model), the joint model demonstrated superior binary mistake-detection performance with an F1@0.5 of 84.1% compared to 80.7%. The joint model showed a significant performance advantage in detecting 'slips,' achieving an F1@0.5 of 56.4% versus 37.5% for the modular pipeline. The authors attribute the modular approach's lower detection accuracy to error propagation between its distinct processing stages.

Both proposed designs outperform existing AEM and ESTANet checkpoints on test videos containing procedural mistakes. The research highlights that joint modeling mitigates the compounding errors inherent in multi-stage modular systems, providing a more robust solution for real-time assistant monitoring during task execution.
takeaways: **Model Performance:** The joint model achieved an 84.1% F1@0.5 score for binary mistake detection, outperforming the modular pipeline's 80.7%.
**Slip Detection:** The joint model significantly improved slip detection, reaching 56.4% F1@0.5 compared to 37.5% in the modular approach.
**Dataset Update:** The researchers repartitioned the EgoPER dataset to include erroneous videos in all splits to support supervised training for mistake detection.
**Benchmark Comparison:** Both the modular and joint models outperformed existing AEM and ESTANet checkpoints on test videos containing procedural errors.

**Error Propagation:** Component-level analysis indicates that the modular approach suffers from performance degradation due to error propagation between its separate identification and verification stages.

title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
author: Nathaniel Cohen, Nicolas Dufour, Amélie Royer, Alasdair Newson
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nathaniel Cohen , Nicolas Dufour , Amélie Royer , Alasdair Newson , Patrick Pérez

Abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

Notes: BMVC 2026. Project page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Nathaniel Cohen, Nicolas Dufour, Amélie Royer, Alasdair Newson, and Patrick Pérez have introduced AURA (AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar), a diffusion-based model designed for low-latency, causal talking-head video generation. Unlike existing bidirectional models that require multi-second audio look-ahead and dozens of denoising steps, AURA utilizes a rolling KV cache to generate video chunk-by-chunk. The model is available in two sizes: AURA 1.3B, which streams 576p video at 20.7 fps, and AURA 5B, which streams 720p video at 9.7 fps, both on a single GPU.

The technical architecture employs a two-stage distillation pipeline. First, a causal student model is trained to match teacher trajectories using a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask and reduced diffusion steps. Second, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation is applied to bridge the quality gap. AURA 1.3B achieves a 23x speedup over its bidirectional teacher, while AURA 5B provides a 17x speedup compared to its teacher, matching TalkVerse performance at 720p. The authors have released the model weights and a dataset of 30,000 synthetic videos with precomputed teacher trajectories to support further research.
takeaways: **Model Variants:** AURA 1.3B (576p at 20.7 fps) and AURA 5B (720p at 9.7 fps).
**Efficiency Gains:** AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its bidirectional teacher; AURA 5B runs 17x faster than its teacher.
**Methodology:** Uses a rolling KV cache and a two-stage distillation pipeline involving causal student alignment and Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD).
**Open Source:** The team released model weights and a 30K synthetic video dataset with precomputed teacher trajectories.
**Conference:** The research is presented at BMVC 2026.

title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models
author: Jiaming Li, Lingzhen Li, Xiaze Yang, Chenyu Zhu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jiaming Li , Lingzhen Li , Xiaze Yang , Chenyu Zhu , Kaiqi Liu , Xiaotong Zhao , Songlian Li , Toyota Li , Alan Zhao , Haobin Zhong , Yue Ma , Zhiyuan Ma

Abstract: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63$\times$ speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.

summary.tldr:
Speculative World Model (SpecWM) is a training-free inference framework designed to optimize video world model performance by replacing traditional verification methods with a latent velocity field-based approach. Developed by a team including Jiaming Li, Lingzhen Li, and others, the framework addresses the inefficiencies of existing speculative decoding, which typically relies on external scorers that incur high computational costs and offer no corrective feedback for rejected drafts. Instead, SpecWM utilizes the target model's latent velocity field to verify draft chunks, allowing for a more efficient selection process categorized into Accept, Refine, or Reject based on two specific thresholds.

The framework introduces a transition-aware refinement mechanism that provides reusable corrections rather than forcing costly target regeneration. One-step refinement is utilized to enhance perceptual quality, while three-step refinement is employed to improve camera following and trajectory consistency. On the WBench Navigation benchmark, SpecWM achieved a 1.63x speedup compared to the target model and improved the NavScore from 75.99 (draft) to 85.63. The authors also introduced LongSpecBench to demonstrate sustained quality and control over extended, multi-turn rollouts, and validated the framework's versatility across various backbones and denoising budgets using the Hy-Nomas dataset.
takeaways: **Performance Metric:** SpecWM achieves a 1.63x speedup over the target model on WBench Navigation.
**Benchmark Improvement:** NavScore increased from 75.99 in the draft model to 85.63 using the SpecWM framework.
**Refinement Methodology:** The system uses one-step refinement for perceptual quality and three-step refinement for camera and trajectory consistency.
**Framework Versatility:** The method is training-free and has been validated across different backbones and varying denoising budgets via the Hy-Nomas dataset.
**Long-term Stability:** LongSpecBench testing confirms the framework maintains quality and control during multi-turn, long-duration rollouts.

title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
author: Shuang Wu, Jiachen Qian, Youtian Lin, Feihu Zhang
contentSnippet: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.

title: A CPU Inside an LLM: Zero-Gradient Compilation of Exact Circuits into Pretrained Weights
author: Tanmay Sah
contentSnippet: Pretrained language models (LMs) remain unreliable on exact multi-digit arithmetic without gradient fine-tuning or external tool interpreters. We introduce closed-form, zero-gradient circuit-grafting primitives that compile deterministic computation directly into pretrained LM weights using zero training examples and zero runtime hooks, while bounding per-layer normalization drift and preserving natural-language (NL) competence. Our construction combines three analytical mechanisms: (1) two-layer Mellin-GLU quadrature over bias-free SwiGLU/GeGLU layers, turning unknown per-token RMSNorm scaling into translation along a log-spaced gate grid (>250times dynamic range) with IEEE 754 error bounds; (2) cross-token scale cancellation via signed Chebyshev Indefinite-RoPE self-sink attention and memoryless SiLU-antisymmetric GatedDeltaNet shifts; and (3) axis-aligned width extension (d to d+K) with d/(d+K) norm compensation, Base-1000 canonical BPE emission, and differential (+254,-256) tied unembeddings. An automated 5-stage compiler synthesizes 4-8 digit signed {+,-,times} circuits in constant TC^0 depth alongside 3-literal Boolean (100%, N=1{,}728; plus 42-layer Gemma 4 E4B audits) and 5-bit Majority/Parity (100%) circuits. title: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era
author: Ilya Gusev
contentSnippet: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. A third ICLR review of a paper added 5.46 new problems to the other two in 2027, against 6.12 in 2026. We apply MELD, a detector of LLM-generated text, to all reviews. Within a paper, two reviews that MELD flags overlap more than two unflagged reviews: by 3.0 points at ICLR in 2024-2025, by 4.5 points in 2026-2027, and by 5.4 points across five journal sources. These results provide evidence that LLM-flagged reviews of one paper are less distinct from each other than unflagged reviews, and suggest that the diversity of critiques among reviews of a single paper is falling.

title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
author: Timo Ropinski, Sebastian Kranz
contentSnippet: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis
author: Andrii Yermakov, Jan Cech, Mario Fritz, Jiri Matas
contentSnippet: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD

title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators
author: Nagham Omar, Rotem Dror, Almog Gueta, Avigdor Gal
contentSnippet: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
author: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu
contentSnippet: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O^{2}LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O^{2}LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O^{2}LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
author: Jiahao Huang, Jun Wang
contentSnippet: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
author: Yang Wan, Linchao Zhu
contentSnippet: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

title: HiUni: Harmonizing Understanding and Generation in Shared Visual Space
author: Jiahao Hu, Jingdong Du, Yichen Zhang, Yi Song
contentSnippet: Unified multimodal models aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single framework. However, prevailing approaches often separate their visual representations or backbone computation to accommodate the different requirements of these two tasks, which limits the degree of unification. In this paper, we present HiUni, which revisits this design choice and explores whether a pretrained vision language model can be directly extended into a unified model with extensive parameter sharing. Specifically, HiUni reuses the same language-aligned ViT and dense Transformer backbone for both capabilities, while confining task-specific computation to the output side. Yet such a design introduces two key challenges. Generation in pixel space is difficult to optimize, and semantic abstraction in pretrained ViT discards fine spatial details required for synthesis. To address these challenges, HiUni introduces a Pixel Diffusion Head tailored to direct pixel-space optimization and a lightweight HiGate pathway that provides fine-grained spatial details near the output stage. Extensive experiments show that HiUni achieves a similar average understanding score to the pretrained VLM while attaining competitive performance on image generation and editing. Controlled comparisons and analyses further demonstrate that a single dense backbone can effectively support both capabilities without task-specific backbone computation, highlighting a simpler path toward unified multimodal modeling.

title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
author: Yingqi Shi, Junru Lu, Yun Liu, Di Yin
contentSnippet: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
author: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara
contentSnippet:
Authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral , Kaan Oktay , Alec Helbling , Atakan Kara , Duen Horng Chau , Pinar Yanardag

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

Notes: Project page: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Researchers Tuna Han Salih Meral et al. demonstrate that reinforcement learning (RL) post-training in diffusion transformers—specifically for visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy—functions primarily as a form of activation steering rather than learning complex, input-dependent transformations. By applying a fixed set of steering vectors to the block outputs of frozen base models, the authors show that these input-independent shifts can replicate the performance gains of traditional RL-tuned models. The study focuses on SD3.5-M, where the steering vectors utilize 65x fewer parameters (0.29M) compared to standard RL-tuned LoRA adapters (18.8M).

Experimental results indicate that these static vectors recover 90.0% to 96.3% of the reward gains across six RL-tuned image models and between 89.8% and 111.9% for two video models. When initialized at zero and trained via online RL, the steering vectors outperformed weight-based RL on specific metrics including text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. The findings suggest that current RL post-training methods for diffusion models are largely steering the pretrained generator toward capabilities it already possesses, rather than developing new, prompt-dependent logic.
takeaways: **Parameter Efficiency:** Steering vectors require only 0.29M parameters, compared to 18.8M for standard RL-tuned LoRA, representing a 65x reduction in parameter count.
**Performance Recovery:** Static steering vectors recover 90.0–96.3% of reward gains for image models and up to 111.9% for video models compared to full RL-tuned checkpoints.

**Methodology:** The vectors are added to the block outputs of frozen base models and are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, proving that input-independent shifts drive the majority of RL gains.
**Benchmark Superiority:** Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the steering vectors outperformed weight-based RL on OCR and PickScore metrics for SD3.5-M.

title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
author: Jacqueline Maasch, Shu Wan, Hank Zhu, Huan Liu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jacqueline Maasch , Shu Wan , Hank Zhu , Huan Liu , Zhiguang Wang

Abstract: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

summary.tldr:
Jacqueline Maasch, Shu Wan, Hank Zhu, Huan Liu, and Zhiguang Wang have introduced Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD), a constraint-based algorithm designed for causal structure learning in multivariate time series. The method addresses common statistical hurdles in time series analysis, such as autocorrelation, distribution shifts, and high dimensionality, by employing a local-to-global learning strategy that sequentially identifies the parent set for each variable.

ITPD leverages temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to reduce computational complexity, specifically by substituting high-order conditional independence tests with lower-order alternatives. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD demonstrated superior efficiency, particularly on large-scale graphs. For networks containing 2,000 nodes, the algorithm achieved speedups of 2.3x over iterative IAMB, 9.1x over DF-PC, and 40.9x over PCMCI, while maintaining a competitive position on the Pareto frontier for F1 scores and wall-clock time.
takeaways: **Algorithm Methodology:** ITPD utilizes a local-to-global approach that sequentially discovers parent sets for individual variables to reconstruct the global causal graph.
**Computational Efficiency:** The algorithm is optimized for large graphs, outperforming baselines like PCMCI by 40.9x on 2,000-node datasets.
**Complexity Reduction:** ITPD minimizes computational overhead by using the local Markov condition to replace high-order conditional independence tests with lower-order alternatives.
**Performance Benchmarks:** The method consistently sits on the Pareto frontier for F1 accuracy and wall-clock execution time compared to existing causal discovery baselines.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
author: Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Zheyuan Liu , Chuhan Wang , Jinduo Guo , Yue Huang , Xiangchi Yuan , Ningshan Ma , Meng Jiang

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

Notes: A two-stage pipeline that teaches VLAs to stop prohibited tasks safely while preserving permitted skills

summary.tldr:
Researchers Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Ningshan Ma, and Meng Jiang have introduced State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI), a two-stage training framework designed to improve safety in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. The method addresses the critical failure mode where robots, even when instructed to stop a prohibited task mid-execution, continue to complete the action or drop held objects, leading to physical incidents. SAFI focuses on teaching robots an explicit, safe alternative response—specifically maintaining a stationary arm position and a consistent gripper state—when a prohibited task is interrupted.

The SAFI pipeline operates through two distinct phases: fallback target construction and joint policy adaptation. In the first stage, the system assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets to demonstrations of prohibited tasks. In the second stage, the model learns these fallback targets alongside the original actions of permitted tasks, ensuring the robot can transition to a safe state without degrading its existing skill set. The authors evaluated the framework using OpenVLA-OFT across the LIBERO and BadLIBERO benchmarks.

Experimental results demonstrate that SAFI significantly improves safety metrics compared to standard VLA training. On evaluated LIBERO tasks, the method reduced the aggregate target success rate after a takeover command to 1.3%. Furthermore, the researchers reported zero physical incidents and no action saturation during testing, confirming that the model can effectively balance safety-critical interventions with the preservation of high performance on permitted tasks.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** SAFI utilizes a two-stage process involving fallback target construction and joint policy adaptation to teach robots safe, stationary responses to prohibited task commands.
**Performance Metric:** In LIBERO task evaluations, SAFI reduced the aggregate target success rate after a mid-execution takeover to 1.3%.
**Safety Outcomes:** The implementation resulted in zero recorded physical incidents and no action saturation during testing phases.
**Model Architecture:** The research utilized OpenVLA-OFT as the base model for testing across LIBERO and BadLIBERO datasets.
**Primary Objective:** The framework specifically addresses the limitation where VLA models fail to safely stop or maintain object control when interrupted during prohibited task execution.

title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
author: Chengkai Xu, Yicheng Guo, Jiaqi Liu, Yiming Cui
contentSnippet:
Authors: Chengkai Xu , Yicheng Guo , Jiaqi Liu , Yiming Cui , Shiyu Fang , Peng Hang , Hao Zhang , Jian Sun

Abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD)}, a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by $3.5$ points on NavTest and $5.0$ points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

summary.tldr:
Researchers Chengkai Xu et al. have introduced Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD), a framework designed to optimize training data selection for end-to-end autonomous driving systems. Unlike traditional methods that rely on intrinsic data properties or generic training proxies, PAD calculates the utility of specific demonstrations relative to a target driving policy. The framework integrates scene-level calibration feedback, projected policy gradients, and a regularized approximation of local training geometry to assign influence-based values to candidate demonstrations, effectively identifying which data points will most benefit a specific planner architecture.

In empirical testing using the DiffusionDrive model, PAD demonstrated significant performance gains over indiscriminate data training. The method improved EPDMS (Expected Planning Deviation Metric Score) by 3.5 points on the NavTest benchmark and 5.0 points on NavHard. The study highlights that data utility is not universal; cross-planner analysis revealed that the same pool of demonstrations yields different rankings when applied to diffusion-based, regression-based, or flow-matching-based planners. By replacing large-scale, indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted curation, PAD reduces scene-level regressions and improves the efficiency of scaling autonomous driving models.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** PAD improved EPDMS scores by 3.5 points on NavTest and 5.0 points on NavHard compared to real-only training.
**Methodological Innovation:** The framework utilizes a combination of scene-level calibration, projected policy gradients, and local training geometry to estimate data utility.
**Planner Specificity:** The research confirms that data value is planner-dependent, with different rankings produced for diffusion, regression, and flow-matching architectures.
**Core Objective:** PAD aims to replace indiscriminate data scaling with targeted curation to minimize redundant or harmful training demonstrations.

title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips
author: Summer Devlin
contentSnippet: At Exa , we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware ( AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2 ), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization. Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving. Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database. Embedding documents at scale Our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices. Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill The preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the new model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices. Optim

summary.tldr:
Exa has optimized its document embedding infrastructure by migrating to AWS Neuron-based hardware, specifically utilizing AWS Inferentia2 and Trainium2 chips. This transition was necessitated by the company's need to re-embed a corpus of 30 billion high-priority documents using a new, superior model, which effectively doubled their inference load. By shifting to this hardware, Exa achieved a 50% increase in embedding throughput, directly improving the unit economics of maintaining a web-scale index that supports both natural language and keyword-based semantic search.

The company's architecture relies on a multi-tower semantic ML model that maps web and query data into a shared vector space. The embedding process is integrated into an asynchronous pipeline that follows crawling, parsing, and moderation stages before data is committed to an in-house vector database. The optimization effort was driven by an agentic development workflow, focusing on maximizing performance-per-dollar to handle the scale of hundreds of billions of documents. This infrastructure allows Exa to minimize the latency between the discovery of new web data and its availability for search and agentic grounding.
takeaways: **Hardware Selection:** Exa migrated its embedding workloads to AWS Inferentia2 and Trainium2 chips to optimize performance-per-dollar.
**Throughput Gains:** The transition to AWS Neuron hardware resulted in a 50% increase in embedding throughput.
**Scale Requirements:** The optimization was triggered by the need to re-embed 30 billion high-priority documents, which temporarily doubled the inference load.
**Architectural Approach:** Exa utilizes multi-tower semantic ML models and an in-house vector database to serve as a foundation for semantic search and agentic grounding.

title: Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:56 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026

Google upgrades Gemini’s agentic Task mode with new model, e-commerce features

Google LLC is releasing a new version of its Gemini artificial intelligence assistant that is better at performing multistep tasks.

Josh Woodward, the vice president responsible for the Gemini app, detailed the update in a Tuesday blog post .

The AI assistant has two modes that are accessible through separate interface tabs. The first, Chat, generates quick, relatively simple responses to prompts. The second mode, which is called Task, enables Gemini to perform complex tasks such as booking appointments and comparing online product listings. Task is the focus of this week’s update.

Google is switching the feature to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, its newest large language model. It’s somewhat less capable than Gemini 4 Carbon, the search giant’s most advanced LLM, but significantly more cost-efficient. Hydrogen is also fast: Google says it can process some tasks 2.8 times faster than its previous entry-level model.

One way Hydrogen reduces wait times is by parallelizing project steps that are usually performed one after another. According to Woodward, users of Gemini’s Task mode can give the model feedback after each step to guide its work. The model proactively asks users for instructions before performing a sensitive task such as making an online purchase.

Today, Gemini’s Task mode uses Google Wallet to process transactions. Woodward said that the search giant is working with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa to add support for a technology called payment tokenization. It replaces the user’s card number with a placeholder value called a token. That token is shared with merchants instead of the card number to reduce the risk of data leaks.

Google also plans to add support for a second technology called the Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP. It makes it easier for AI agents such as Gemini to interact with online stores and thereby lowers the risk of errors.

Gemini’s Task mode can use data in other Google services such as Gmail to inform its decisions. For example, the agent might take the user’s past purchases into account when generating shopping suggestions. One of Gemini’s main selling points is that it can use such data without moving it off Google infrastructure, which is often not the case with competing agents.

“When you assign Gemi

summary.tldr:
Google has updated its Gemini assistant's 'Task' mode, transitioning the feature to the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen large language model. While positioned as less capable than the flagship Gemini 4 Carbon, Hydrogen is optimized for cost-efficiency and speed, reportedly processing tasks 2.8 times faster than the previous entry-level model. The update focuses on agentic capabilities, allowing Gemini to execute multistep workflows such as appointment booking and e-commerce product comparisons through a parallelized processing architecture.

To enhance security and reliability in agentic commerce, Google is integrating payment tokenization in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, replacing card numbers with secure placeholders. Additionally, the company is adopting the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) to standardize agent-to-merchant interactions. Gemini’s Task mode operates within Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine, utilizing hardware-isolated, sandboxed virtual machines dedicated to individual user accounts to ensure data remains within Google infrastructure during processing.

Google has made the updated Task mode free for users in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India. This move directly challenges the subscription-based agentic features offered by competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic, potentially pressuring those firms to adjust their pricing models.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** Gemini Task mode now utilizes Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which features parallelized step execution to achieve a 2.8x speed improvement over the prior entry-level model.
**Security Infrastructure:** Agentic tasks run on Google Cloud’s Agent Compute Engine, utilizing hardware-isolated, sandboxed virtual machines that are not shared between users.
**Commerce Integration:** Google is implementing payment tokenization with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa, alongside the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) to reduce transaction errors.

**Market Availability:** The updated Task mode is currently free in the U.S., Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India, positioning it as a direct competitor to paid agentic offerings from Anthropic and OpenAI.

title: Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected
author: Mike Wheatley
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 18:50 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO priced at $83 per share, higher than expected

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic PBC today priced one of the most eagerly anticipated initial public offerings in history at a price of $83 per share, setting the stage for the biggest stock market listing ever.

The pricing, which has been reported by multiple news outlets including Bloomberg , Reuters and the Financial Times , is even higher than the company’s expected range of $70 to $78 per share.

If that price is correct, and if Anthropic sells all of its shares, it would raise in excess of $68 billion from the sale. Including the $26 billion in private placements, that puts Anthropic’s offering at more than $94 billion, surpassing even Space Exploration Technologies Corp. blockbuster $86 billion listing back in June.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last week, Anthropic had said its expected price range would give it a valuation of $1.4 trillion, but its market capitalization could well be even higher than that. The company’s shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.” Its debut might help the AI industry to push back against growing concerns that it’s entering into unsustainable bubble territory after years of breathtaking technological advances that has seen investors pour billions of dollars into almost any AI bet they can.

The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has recently been beset by numerous setbacks , including the U.S. population’s backlash against data center building that was evident during the midterm elections, and then the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang last week. Those events raised concerns even higher in a market that was already jittery about the prospect of rising interest rates that could put debt financing out of the reach of many smaller AI infrastructure companies.

Some of the technology industry’s biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as customers, partners and shareholders. For instance, both Amazon.com Inc. and Google LLC have sizable stakes in the company, and others including Microsoft Corp., Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. have invested billions into its IPO. Meanwhile, the company is one of the biggest buyers of AI chips from those firms.

“If we do this right,

summary.tldr:
Anthropic PBC has priced its initial public offering at $83 per share, exceeding its previously stated range of $70 to $78. This valuation sets the company up for a potential market capitalization of $1.4 trillion, with the offering expected to raise over $68 billion in share sales, plus an additional $26 billion in private placements. The company is scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange this Thursday under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

Financially, Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine-month period ending September 30, 2026, representing a 1,200% year-over-year increase. Despite this growth, the company recorded a $104 billion net loss for the same period, largely attributed to adjustments in the value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. As of October 2026, the company reached a revenue run-rate of $81 billion. Analysts project revenue to reach $53 billion by the end of the current fiscal year, with forecasts climbing to between $270 billion and $280 billion by 2028.
takeaways: **IPO Pricing:** Shares are priced at $83, surpassing the expected $70–$78 range and positioning the company for a $1.4 trillion valuation.
**Financial Performance:** Revenue reached $33.24 billion for the first nine months of 2026, with a net loss of $104 billion driven by accounting adjustments for convertible notes.
**Revenue Projections:** Analysts estimate fiscal year 2027 revenue between $135 billion and $137 billion, scaling to $270–$280 billion by 2028.
**Strategic Backing:** Major investors and partners include Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD, all of which have significant financial exposure to the company.
**Market Context:** The IPO serves as a benchmark for the AI sector, occurring amidst industry volatility and following the recent ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
author: Lucas Ropek
contentSnippet:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.

“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”

In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.

The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.

Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”

“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.

“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”

Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.

“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made

summary.tldr:
At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella highlighted the systemic security risks posed by 'unpatchable' critical infrastructure, specifically citing firmware in HVAC systems, data center chillers, and transportation networks that are connected to the internet. Nadella argued that the widespread 'smartification' of legacy hardware has created a massive, vulnerable attack surface that is increasingly susceptible to AI-aided cyberattacks.

Nadella noted that while AI tools have accelerated the discovery of software vulnerabilities, they have simultaneously compressed the remediation timeline. This creates a 'perfect storm' where organizations are forced to deploy patches into production almost instantly to counter active exploitation, leading to increased operational instability. Regarding recent service disruptions, including the Microsoft Outlook outage, Nadella characterized the event as a 'latent bug' and committed to implementing both upstream architectural and operational fixes to prevent recurrence.
takeaways: **Infrastructure Vulnerability:** Critical systems including HVAC units and data center chillers are frequently running on unpatchable firmware while remaining connected to the internet.

**Remediation Pressure:** The use of AI to identify vulnerabilities has forced companies to move from testing and validation to immediate production deployment, increasing the risk of system instability.
**Outlook Incident:** Microsoft attributed the recent global Outlook outage to a 'latent bug' that resulted in a 'perfect storm' of operational failure.
**Strategic Shift:** Nadella emphasized the need for modernization and the development of real-time detection and defense capabilities to counter the evolving threat landscape.

title: Elon Musk says ousting Jensen Huang is like ‘kicking Michael Jordan off your team’
author: Amanda Silberling
contentSnippet:
Elon Musk has already been vocal about his disapproval of the Nvidia board’s decision to oust its founder and CEO Jensen Huang after a series of extramarital affairs were made public, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who is suspected of feeding sensitive information back to Beijing. At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk elaborated on his thoughts about Nvidia’s leadership change.

“Jensen is an old friend of mine,” Musk said. “I would call Jensen, you know, Michael Jordan at his peak level, in terms of what he means to a team.”

On X, the social media platform he owns, Musk even said he would hire Huang.

“He’s one of the most talented entrepreneur-CEOs in history,” Musk said when asked about his X post. “Who wouldn’t want to hire Jensen?”

Musk also signed a petition , alongside over 200,000 other people, urging Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO. Nvidia’s board, however, confirmed it is not planning to bring Huang back.

“[It] doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me…,” Musk said of that decision. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.”

He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades,” Musk added. “He understands technology incredibly well. His team loves him… and many of them are there because of him, and have higher offers to go elsewhere, and have turned them down because of personal loyalty to Jensen.”

Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey also said that he thinks Nvidia is making the wrong decision by not reinstating Huang.

“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said earlier in the day at the DealBook event. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.”

Musk also did not express concern over what Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could mean for U.S. national security.

“I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States,” Musk said. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders.”

Other peers in the industry, like Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its founder and CEO of 33 years at the helm.

“It’s the Nvidia board’s decision, but I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella said at DealBook. “

summary.tldr:
Elon Musk and other prominent tech figures have publicly criticized the Nvidia board’s decision to terminate founder and CEO Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit, Musk compared Huang’s departure to "kicking Michael Jordan off your team" during a winning streak, arguing that the leadership change is detrimental to shareholder value and ignores Huang’s unique technical expertise and long-standing industry relationships. Musk has signed a petition, which has garnered over 200,000 signatures, calling for Huang’s reinstatement.

Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey echoed Musk’s sentiment, suggesting that Huang’s removal serves the interests of China and weakens U.S. technological standing, noting that the leadership turmoil has already resulted in a $1 trillion decline in Nvidia’s market capitalization. Conversely, other industry leaders, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have expressed confidence in Nvidia’s future. Nadella specifically endorsed interim CEO Colette Kress, a former Microsoft executive, citing her professional capabilities and the strength of the remaining Nvidia team. Despite the external pressure, Nvidia’s board has confirmed it has no plans to reinstate Huang, who led the company for 33 years.
takeaways: **Leadership Transition:** Nvidia’s board has officially confirmed it will not reinstate Jensen Huang following his termination over personal conduct issues.
**Market Impact:** Palmer Luckey stated that the leadership crisis has contributed to a $1 trillion reduction in Nvidia’s market capitalization.
**Industry Support:** A petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement has surpassed 200,000 signatures, with Elon Musk among the high-profile signatories.
**Executive Endorsements:** Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella publicly expressed confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress and the broader Nvidia organization.
**Security Allegations:** The termination followed reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an individual suspected of feeding sensitive information to Beijing.

title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.” Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.” In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.” Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

summary.tldr:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago public school districts are considering abandoning Google Search after Google announced that starting next year, schools will be unable to disable Gemini-powered AI features without also losing access to Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, defended the move by stating that Search and AI are deeply integrated, leaving districts that reject AI without access to Google Search.

The policy triggered severe backlash from elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani—who recently banned AI use for students in grades 2 through 8—and Senator Bernie Sanders, both of whom characterized Google's ultimatum as extortion. New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels and Chicago public schools officials stated they will actively explore alternative search solutions if Google does not reverse its position.

In response to educator concerns regarding student critical thinking and learning shortcuts, Google spokesperson Laura Breen noted that the company is piloting Guided Learning capabilities to provide step-by-step problem-solving rather than direct answers. Google also stated that upcoming control updates will make Gemini apps, Gemini Notebook, and Search off by default until schools explicitly enable them. However, transitioning away from Google remains logistically challenging given how deeply embedded Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and related services are across US classrooms.
takeaways: **Affected School Districts:** New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago public schools are evaluating alternatives to Google Search.
**Google's Policy Change:** Starting next year, schools cannot disable Gemini-powered AI features without simultaneously losing access to Google Search.
**Political Backlash:** Officials including NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders publicly condemned Google's policy as 'extortion'.
**Product Adjustments:** Google is piloting Guided Learning features to walk students through problems step-by-step and will make Gemini and Search off by default until schools opt in.

title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
author: Amanda Silberling
contentSnippet:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies .

“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.

While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.

“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”

Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.

“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”

Huang, who led Nvidia for 33 years, resigned following reports of an affair with an executive at Megaspeed—a company allegedly linked to Chinese intelligence—as well as additional affairs with two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.

Despite the leadership transition, Nadella expressed continued confidence in Nvidia, citing his professional history with interim CEO Colette Kress, who previously held a tenure at Microsoft. Nadella emphasized that while founders are instrumental in creating companies, they are not infallible, noting that organizational success requires transition planning beyond the original leadership.
